nary.participants: k files and the entities in them, message, PR, date
nary.model: ChangeSet node, `touches` edges with a role (added, modified, deleted) and hunk spans. Walk weight `w/(set size)`, or ROSE-style rules between entity *sets*
nary.loses: Which pairs were two of thirty; the commit's reason (message) and PR; the order and time of the set. k(k-1)/2 edges per commit instead of k
nary.evidence: 85% of used commits touch more than 2 files; commits of 16 to 30 files are 12% of commits and 55% of pair incidences; 49% of co-change edges rest only on commits of 10 or more files (section 3.2). ROSE's own mitigation is a size cap; Zhou's walk is the principled weight

nary.participants: statement, conditions, exemptions, anchors in different roles (server guard, client half, dependent rule), rationale
nary.model: Rule node; `constrains` edges with a role property; `justified_by` edges; `depends_on` between rules

nary.evidence: The bill-freeze group spans server and client at group level; two bullets span runtimes by direct anchors (schema lane); v1 edges carry only `token` and `how`

nary.participants: statement, and the set of spans, hashes and negative facts ("no other caller") it rests on

nary.loses: The set as a unit: a pairwise `rests_on` is fine as long as all members are present; the point of the node is that the Claim has a status and a producer
nary.evidence: Replay of cached answers (K0): 0 stale answers on 29,097 lookups with fact-level dependencies against 6.5% stale with file-level (v1 audit). Provenance semirings: the footprint is a set of sets (why-provenance)

refute.verdict:
The design is a real improvement on v1, but its claim that every choice comes from documented theory does not hold yet. It starts from the measured questions, names its sources, carries the verifiers' corrections and keeps the agent pilot as the only test of tokens. Four problems remain.

1. Improvised choices and miscited sources remain:
   - About a dozen thresholds have no source.
   - The M3 role vocabulary is hand-made.
   - S2's stop rule uses the wrong value for F: 695 tokens is what a scripted search read per typed question. Counting the carry over the remaining calls, an avoided search is worth about 13,000 tokens.
   - Three sources are cited for things they do not say:
     - Hogan's knowledge-graph definition is inclusive, so v1 was already a knowledge graph.
     - The in-lists and out-lists cited to de Kleer belong to Doyle's JTMS.
     - S2's "own derivation" is in fact the marginal value theorem and the information patch model.
2. The validation plan drops the use-case lane's own test set: CQ instances taken from transcripts and weighted by carried tokens. So the zero-model evidence again scores co-change truth and hand-written typed questions, not the measured use. The whole ranking stack serves a question that is not among the 16 recorded CQs.
3. Several tuning tests cannot fail, or are biased:
   - The M1 coverage check and the M6 "cut by about a third" rule pass by construction.
   - The Q1 prune test leans toward cutting kinds.
   - The M3 replay leans toward passing.
   - The A1 brief test passes on file names alone.
   - T4 has no threshold.
   - K1, S1, R4 and R5 have no cut rule.
   - R1 re-runs the pilot on the same 65 commits, without the scripted-search arm an agent actually uses.
   - No clean confirmation set remains: the 75 held-out commits are spent, and only 16 commits (10 touching product code) exist after the frozen commit.
4. The decisive agent pilot, as round 2 sized it (about 40 tasks), detects only savings of about 20 to 25 %. The design's own illustration is 3 to 5 % of product context.

Leak paths the design does not close:
- Hand-assigned invariant roles taken from today's CLAUDE.md text, which names later migrations and PRs.
- Held-out-period snapshots inside the "tuning data".
- In-sample transcript replays: the same 13 sessions produced the question list and would score the brief.

Most program documents are off the commit history: 1,780 untracked files against 124 tracked. So T1/T4 cannot cover most of the 1,147M program carried tokens, and CQ1 conclusions mostly rest on unverifiable premises such as papers, web pages and scratch measurements.

Components that hold up: the storage choice, the not-worth-it list, A1's no-query-language/no-paging stance, K1/K2/K5/K6, T2/T5 and the R1 measurement itself.

findings.title: Hogan's definition of a knowledge graph is misquoted
findings.detail: The design defines a knowledge graph as "a graph with a schema, stable identity, provenance and quality measures [Hogan]". Hogan et al. (ACM CSUR 2021, arXiv 2003.02320, introduction, text extracted from the PDF) adopt an inclusive definition: a graph of data intended to accumulate and convey knowledge of the real world, whose nodes are entities and whose edges are relations. Schema, identity and context are topics the survey discusses, and quality is one of its methods; none is definitional. Consequence: by Hogan's own definition v1 was already a knowledge graph. v2 adds the aspects Hogan discusses. The answer to the owner's "strictly graphs or knowledge graphs or TKGs" must say that.
findings.ruling: R-1 (the knowledge-graph wording: v1 already was one in Hogan’s inclusive sense)

findings.title: "Not a temporal knowledge graph" is too narrow, and so is "is a TKG"
findings.detail: A temporal knowledge graph in the representation sense is a set of facts annotated with time (quadruples or validity intervals). T1's validity sets over commits are exactly that, with the difference that time here is a partial order (the commit graph branches), not a line. What v2 is not is a TKG in the completion or forecasting sense (TLogic, RE-Net). Round 2's temporal lane says it did not review the TKG literature (`../widen/lane-temporal.md` line 51), so neither round has a primary source for the representation sense either. This is a wording fix, but it is the owner's own question.
findings.ruling: R-1 (say which sense of temporal knowledge graph is meant)

findings.title: [deKleer] is cited for in-lists and out-lists
findings.detail: In-lists and out-lists are the support-list justifications of Doyle's justification-based truth maintenance system (1979). De Kleer's 1986 assumption-based system works with assumption sets and labels. The time lane got this right ("JTMS justifications with in and out lists (Doyle 1979)", `lane-time-incremental.md` line 302, with Doyle not opened and described through de Kleer). The design's citation should read Doyle (not opened), described in de Kleer 1986. Nothing in M4 needs either system's machinery; what M4 actually uses is the verifying trace of Build Systems a la Carte (confirmed, verify-b T-a).
findings.ruling: R-1 (cite Doyle; the ledger uses build-system traces)

findings.title: S2's stop rule is called "the lane's own derivation", but there is documented theory for it, and the number plugged into it is the wrong quantity
findings.ruling: R-1 and R-2 (the stop rule now cites the marginal value theorem; it stays a trial and the calibration it needs is cut unless it survives first)

Restart 0.15 matches Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg's rooted PageRank setting (confirmed, verify-b R-a), but that is a different graph and task; the design sweeps it anyway, which is right.

findings.title: Q1 prune test: biased toward cutting, and measuring the wrong thing
findings.detail: Removing a kind and checking T1 recall plus 20 typed questions cannot show the value of a kind that serves a CQ with one or two questions (uses_fixture for CQ7, for example). With paired SD 0.263 on recall, "recall falls beyond the 95 % interval" will almost never happen, so the rule prunes by absence of evidence. It also contradicts the forward check (every kind serves some CQ). Fix: decide kinds by the backward check per CQ (can the CQ still be answered without the kind) on enough questions per CQ, and use recall only for the ranking kinds.
findings.ruling: R-4 (a), (i): decide kinds by per-question answerability

findings.title: M1 test (a) cannot fail
findings.detail: Adding nodes for variables and members raises "share of definitions with a node" by construction. It is a build check. Also the baseline 88.8 % is the held-out figure (354 of 3,150); the tuning figure is 91.3 % (364 of 4,162 missing, `v1-audit.md`), so the test quotes the wrong set.

findings.title: M3 test (ii) is biased toward passing
findings.detail: "Sections later cited or acted on" is measured from transcripts in which only 9 % of model calls carry visible text (`use-cases.md` §11), so use is under-observed and the read-but-unused share looks larger than it is.
findings.ruling: R-4 (d), (e): content-based scoring and stronger competitors

findings.detail: "The card contains the files and sections the session went on to edit or cite" is met by a list of names, which costs a few tokens; the agent then still reads the files. The test must score the tokens the agent would still have to read after the card, or count containment of the needed spans' content, not of their names. Its strongest simple arm is missing: the phase's own sections pulled by heading and ID with `awk` (what agents already do) or an orchestrator-written brief.

findings.ruling: R-4 (i): a cut rule is required

findings.title: R1 test lacks the agent-realistic baseline
findings.detail: The declared arms are plain co-change, v1 final and rule pick, PPR, directory proximity, F and L. The scripted search arm (grep for the seed's identifiers plus the co-change and directory tails) is missing, although it is the one v1 failed to beat outside the mobile app and the one an agent actually runs. Without it R1 can pass while losing to what an agent does today.
findings.ruling: R-4 (c): the scripted-search arm is added

findings.title: R4 and R5 have no margin
findings.detail: "Paired contrast with and without" and "cut if not higher" need the same 0.02 P@10 or 0.065 recall resolution and an interval rule as R1.
findings.ruling: R-4 (i): a margin is required

findings.title: T2 "stale must be 0" is sound but bounded
findings.detail: Zero stale is judged against the extractor's own facts (`v1-audit.md`, k0 row). The mutation test removes or adds one fact at a time; it does not test multi-fact interactions or extractor misses. A cached answer can be fresh and wrong.
findings.ruling: R-1: zero stale is relative to the extractor’s facts

findings.detail: ("non-trivial share", "nearly everything"). It can neither pass nor fail as written.
findings.ruling: R-4 (i): a number is required

findings.title: S1 test has no cut rule
findings.detail: A reliability curve and Brier score are reported, not judged.
findings.ruling: R-2: calibration is cut unless the stop rule survives

findings.title: The ranking tests re-use the data that chose the arms
findings.detail: The pilot (`lane-ranking.md` §5) ran on exactly the 65 tuning commits and the late 50 rolling split. RRF with k = 60, restart 0.15, the 2-feature form and the floor were all seen there. R1's "keep F only if its paired interval over the best simpler arm is above zero and the gain is at least 0.02" will be computed on the same commits, where RRF already beat the graph-conditioned floor by about +0.022 (0.233 against 0.211). This is a re-run, not a test. The held-out 75 are spent and only 16 commits (10 touching product code) exist after the frozen commit `a31924a` (2026-08-03), checked with `git rev-list`. No clean confirmation of any ranking choice is possible on zero-model data. The design should say so in R1, not only in section 10.
findings.ruling: R-4 (i) and R-7 (no clean confirmation set remains for ranking; ranking is moved last)

findings.title: Rolling origin is sound for history features, and only for them
findings.detail: The pilot builds features from the parent snapshot (`feat.py` line 25, verify-b R-o). Training on at least 15 earlier commits and scoring the late 50 is a correct time-respecting split. Ridge with at most 8 features on about 15,000 candidate rows will not overfit in the classical sense, but the rows are clustered (388 seeds in 50 commits), so the effective sample is about 50, and 12 R2 variants chosen on an inner split then compared on the outer 50 still invite a winner's curse unless the comparison is nested and reported with the selection step inside the bootstrap.
findings.ruling: R-4 (i) (nested selection inside the bootstrap)

findings.title: Document text written after the fact is a leak path the design does not close
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md's invariants name later migrations and PRs (for example migration 0046 and PRs #162 and #163), so many of them did not exist at early tuning commits. M3's role anchors are "hand-assigned once for the 20 invariants", at the current text. If any M3 fact (a rule anchor, a "same rule" feature, a `brief` section) is used when scoring a tuning commit, it carries knowledge of later defects into the past. The rule must be: every document fact used at commit C is extracted from the document as of C, and hand-assigned roles are dated and used only from their date.
findings.ruling: R-4 (h) (leak rule)

findings.title: The program documents are not on the code's history at all
findings.detail: 124 files under `docs/program` are tracked (on a docs branch, not main) and 1,780 are untracked (checked with `git ls-files`). Program work is 1,147M carried tokens, almost five times product work. T1's commit-keyed validity cannot apply to most of it; the design names this only as an owner decision ("index by content hash"). Two histories (code commits, and document versions by hash) have to be modelled, and T5 citations cross them.
findings.ruling: R-4 (g) (two histories)

findings.title: The "tuning data" definition includes snapshots from the held-out period
findings.detail: The 191 cached snapshots cover the whole history, held-out commits included. Using them for the identity replay (M6) and the invalidation tests (T2, T5) is harmless, because those tests score no retrieval. Using them for T6's "find the next changed files more often than recency alone" would spend held-out commits again. The design should restrict every predictive test to the tuning range.
findings.ruling: R-4 (h) (predictive tests stay in the tuning range)

findings.title: The transcript replays are in-sample
findings.detail: The 13 product sessions (one day, 2026-11-13, one plan) produced the CQ list, the 55 % session-start figure and the `brief` idea; the `brief` and M3 replays then score on the same 13 sessions. Those sessions also ran on code three months after the frozen commit, and transcripts carry no commit SHA (`use-cases.md` §11), so the replay must first establish which commit each session saw.
findings.ruling: R-4 (a) and R-7 (the replay must first establish which commit each session saw)

findings.title: The transcript-derived, carried-token-weighted CQ test set
findings.detail: (section 6). Without it no zero-model number is about the measured use.

findings.title: An index-only arm
findings.detail: , in the zero-model tests and in the pilot: section outline, ID lookup, symbol and file index and BM25, with no relation edges. The pilot's BM25-only arm is close but lacks outlines and IDs. This is the ablation that shows whether the graph part, rather than the index part, saves tokens. Uschold and Gruninger (confirmed, verify-a M1) say CQs cannot rank two designs that both answer them; this arm is how the design ranks "graph" against "index".

findings.title: Programmer-navigation and task-context theory as the source for `brief`
A push mechanism with its own test
findings.detail: `use-cases.md` §7 point 5 says the "is this still true" check must be pushed at edit time, because agents trust documents and never ask. The design mentions an edit-time warning in T5 and CQ4 but has no component for the hook (what triggers it, its token cost per edit, its false-alarm rate). Round 2 found that adoption needs steering (CodeCompass: 51 of 88 graph-condition trials, 58 %, made no graph call; a checklist raised adoption to 100 % in one group, with the prompt changed, W; `../widen/lane-agents.md`).

Round 2 records one pre-registered small-model study where localisation gains were explained better by the embedding index than by the graph (`../widen/lane-agents.md` line 119, W). For prose lookups (CQ1, CQ2) an embedding arm is the obvious competitor to BM25. It should be listed with its install size so the owner can decide.

findings.detail: (section 9), and an intermediate lookup-level replay (tokens per answered lookup on recorded lookups, with and without the tool's answer) that can see effects of a few percent.

claims.claim: v2 is a knowledge graph in Hogan's sense because it has a schema, stable identity, provenance and quality measures
claims.detail: Hogan et al. 2021 (introduction, PDF text extracted) use an inclusive definition: a graph of data meant to accumulate and convey knowledge, with entity nodes and relation edges. Schema, identity, context and quality are aspects the survey discusses, not requirements. By that definition v1 was already a knowledge graph; v2 adds the aspects.

claims.claim: v2 is not a temporal knowledge graph
claims.detail: It is a TKG in the representation sense (facts with validity over a branching commit history). It is not a TKG in the forecasting or completion sense (TLogic, RE-Net). Neither research round reviewed the representation-sense TKG literature.

claims.claim: The CQs a graph can serve carry 38% of product carried tokens (8.8% of product context) and about 21% of program context
claims.detail: The arithmetic checks (91.9M of 242M). The program figure leans on CQ1 (521M), which has the noisiest label, and its conclusions mostly rest on papers, web pages and scratch measurements that T4 cannot check.

claims.claim: Illustration: v2 could move about 3-5% of product context and about 8% of program context
claims.detail: Correctly labelled as an illustration. It must never be stated as a forecast, and it is far below what the planned pilot can detect: round 2's power script needs about a 20-25% per-task saving for 80% power at about 40 tasks.

claims.claim: CodexGraph used 7-15x the tokens of BM25 for equal or slightly better results
claims.detail: Confirmed by verify-a (M5). One system, GPT-4o only.

claims.claim: Q1: store the CQ registry as data, with forward and backward checks
claims.detail: The registry is sound. The kind-prune test (recall must fall beyond the paired 95% interval on T1 plus 20 typed questions) cannot show the value of a kind that serves a CQ with only 1-2 questions, so it prunes by absence of evidence. Decide kinds by per-CQ answerability instead.

claims.claim: M1 closes the 11.2% definition gap (from 88.8% to over 97%)
claims.detail: The test cannot fail: adding nodes for variables and members raises coverage by construction. 88.8% is the held-out figure; the tuning baseline is 91.3% (364 of 4,162 missing).

claims.claim: M1: drop references_literal if under a third of recorded usage searches target a literal
claims.detail: The threshold has no source. CQ8 in total is 4.2% of product carried tokens.

claims.claim: M2/K4 tiers 1-2 give exact field contracts
claims.detail: Run them as a trial behind the K4 test. CQ13 is only 1.0% of product carried tokens (2.4M) and 2.9M of program.

claims.claim: K4 tier 3: a def-use pass over untyped web JavaScript
claims.detail: It rests on one abstract (ARISE: one backbone, weak) and costs days for under 1% of carried tokens. Not worth building.

claims.claim: M3 meaning layer is the largest candidate saving
claims.detail: It is the largest addressable cost (CQ2 plus CQ4: 17% of product, 22% of program), not a saving. The 55% session-start share includes code orientation, so it is not M3's share. Most of that cost can be reached by an outline-and-ID index or by orchestrator-written briefs, with no relations.

claims.claim: M3 constrains edges carry theory-derived roles (guard, client half, condition input, example, violation)
claims.detail: The W3C n-ary note justifies making a rule a node. It says nothing about which roles; the role vocabulary is hand-made.

claims.claim: M3 tuning test (ii): if sections later cited or acted on exceed half of what was read, demote the layer
claims.detail: Use is measured from transcripts where only 9% of model calls carry visible text. Use is under-observed, so the test leans toward passing.

claims.claim: M4 ledger: no stale conclusion is served
claims.detail: This holds only for conclusions whose premises are in the repository, and 'stale' is judged against the extractor's facts. How often conclusions are reused is unmeasured, and the nearby evidence is flat to negative.

claims.claim: M4 theory: justifications with in-lists and out-lists [deKleer]
claims.detail: In-lists and out-lists are Doyle's 1979 JTMS; the time lane itself says so. M4 actually rests on Build Systems a la Carte's verifying traces.

claims.claim: M5 change set as a hyperedge answers the 'and why' of CQ6/CQ10
claims.detail: In effect it is `git log -- path`. No ranking gain is expected; it costs hours.

claims.claim: M6 stable identity is the precondition for stored conclusions and citations
claims.detail: Its cut condition (cut spurious invalidations by about a third) re-measures a known 34% (736 of 2,179 vanished ids are line-number moves). Its value depends on M4 conclusions being reused, which is untested.

claims.claim: M7 splits evidence and confidence per method class
claims.detail: Hygiene only; parser-exact kinds are already about 1.0. Fold it into the K6 quality card.

claims.claim: K1 framework export gives exact routes and schemas
claims.detail: There is no cut rule ('each difference read by hand'). Pin the FastAPI version (verify-a C6).

claims.claim: K2: keep type-aware resolution; mypy residue is a trial
claims.detail: Calls already use no name-only resolution (0 of 4,886).

claims.claim: K3 extraction audit decides whether extraction is a bottleneck
claims.detail: Extraction is already strong (sampled call precision 30 of 30) and the audit needs installs. Defer it until a CQ-level test points to missing edges.

claims.claim: K6 quality card per build
claims.detail: Its seeded-error test can fail.

claims.claim: T1 validity sets give correct as-of answers (71x fewer records)
claims.detail: No CQ asks an 'as of commit K' question, and the saving is disk, which costs nothing here. T1 is harness infrastructure. Most program documents (1,780 untracked against 124 tracked) are not on the commit history.

claims.claim: T2: zero stale cached answers by construction
claims.detail: Zero stale is relative to the extractor's own facts. The mutation test changes one fact at a time; a cached answer can be fresh and still wrong.

claims.claim: T3 kind-level relevance filter
claims.detail: It has no token effect, and fact-level validation already takes 0.31 ms per snapshot. Not worth building.

claims.claim: T4 ledger revalidation with statuses
claims.detail: Test (ii) states no threshold ('non-trivial share'). Most program conclusions fall in the unverifiable class.

claims.claim: T5 citation resolution fact
claims.detail: It must model two histories: code commits, and document versions by hash.

claims.claim: T6 since-view is smaller than git diff --stat and finds the next changed files more often than recency alone
claims.detail: Its predictive test must stay within the tuning commits. The 191 snapshots include the held-out period.

claims.claim: R1: RRF of PPR and co-change beats PPR by +0.030 P@10 [+0.015, +0.044]
claims.detail:
The measurement holds (verify-b reproduced it). As a test it is weak:
- The 'keep' test re-runs the pilot on the same 65 commits.
- It omits the scripted-search arm that an agent actually uses.
- Its truth (co-modified files) is not among the 16 recorded CQs.

claims.claim: R1: 25 features tie 2
claims.detail: +0.001 [-0.007, +0.009], reproduced by verify-b.

claims.claim: GNNs, KG embeddings, LambdaMART and TLogic are not worth it at this size
claims.detail: Pujara's evidence covers translational models from 2013-16; for modern models the conclusion is a medium-strength inference.

claims.claim: R2: rebuild co-change as a weighted projection (NBI, smoothing, cap, half-life)
claims.detail: NBI's gain was measured on randomly split MovieLens data (85,250 links). Here it is one variant among 12 and needs nested selection to avoid a winner's curse.

claims.claim: R3: a depth-3 tier raises the pool ceiling from 71.3% to 92.3%
claims.detail: It serves the minor co-change truth. Defer it.

claims.claim: R4: lexical entry, worth 19 points against about 2 for traversal (LocAgent)
claims.detail: That ablation is a fine-tuned 7B on an unnamed dataset: direction only. The test has no margin.

claims.claim: R5: what-breaks ranker on failing tests
claims.detail: Research-scale cost (differential test runs over 89 commits) for part of CQ8's 4.2%. Legunsen's figures are revision shares, from Java. Defer it.

claims.claim: S1: isotonic calibration is a prerequisite for S2/S3
claims.detail: It is needed only if S2 survives. Rank-position precision on earlier commits is cheaper. The test has no cut rule.

claims.claim: S2: value-density stop below 1/F with F about 695 tokens
claims.detail: The theory exists: Charnov's marginal value theorem and Pirolli and Card's patch model. But 695 is what a scripted search read per typed lookup question, not the cost of finding an omitted file. Counting the carry, it is about 13,000 tokens, at which the stop almost never fires.

claims.claim: S3: level of detail per node by tree knapsack
claims.detail: Keep as a trial. Its source is the information diet model.

claims.claim: S4: connect via exact Steiner tree
claims.detail: No recorded CQ asks how named entities connect. Not worth building.

claims.claim: S5: MMR redundancy term
claims.detail: Not worth a component. Keep the share as a measurement inside the A1 size test; the only published packer won 1 of 14 contrasts.

claims.claim: A1: one CLI with no query language and no paging
claims.detail: CypherBench best 61.58%; iterative paging scored 12.0% against 15.7% with no search tool.

claims.claim: A1 caps: 1,000 tokens by default, 2,000 hard
claims.detail: The cited caps come from a study of models up to 32B. They are untested for frontier agents.

claims.claim: A1 brief test: holds later-edited files and sections in at least 70% of phase starts at no more than a quarter of the tokens
claims.detail: A list of names passes it while saving nothing. Score the content the agent would still have to read, and add the strongest simple arms: heading and ID extraction, and an orchestrator-written brief.

claims.claim: A2: tree format is 0.43x the tokens of triples
claims.detail: For size only. The accuracy evidence is about one sample out of 37.

claims.claim: A3: pointer of at most 500 tokens, about 0.35% of tokens
claims.detail: Adoption needs steering beyond a pointer: in CodeCompass, 58% of graph-condition trials made no graph call.

claims.claim: ST1: SQLite plus in-process arrays; no graph database
claims.detail: At this size. Revisit at about 10^5 nodes.

claims.claim: Section 9: not worth it at this size
claims.detail: GRAIL's own small sets (3.6k-39k nodes) support it.

claims.claim: Validation plan: rolling origin, paired bootstrap, declared arms, one-standard-error rule
claims.detail: It drops the transcript-derived, carried-token-weighted CQ test set. No clean confirmation set remains. Document facts must be taken as of each commit.

claims.claim: The held-out commits are spent; one run is reported as descriptive only
claims.detail: Only 16 commits (10 touching product code) exist after the frozen commit a31924a (2026-08-03).

claims.claim: The agent pilot is the decisive test
claims.detail: At about 40 tasks it has 0.02-0.09 power at a true 10% saving. It cannot see the design's own 3-5% illustration. Focus the pilot on tasks the served CQs dominate, or add a lookup-level replay.

claims.claim: The owner-words table covers every phrase honestly
claims.detail:
These need plain wording:
- 'Semantic relations': v2 has no meaning-similarity retrieval.
- 'Spatial topology': it is only the folder tree and the slice quotient.
- 'Temporal': mostly harness infrastructure.
- 'Knowledge graph' and 'TKG': need the Hogan and two-sense corrections.

claims.claim: 12b: earlier rounds never treated ranking as link prediction, selection as knapsack, identity or n-ary modelling
claims.detail: But v2 repeats round 1's habit of validating mainly on co-change truth.

rulings.title: Honest source labels
rulings.text: The refuter is right that not every choice has a source yet. Each component is shown with one of four honest labels: "from a named source", "simplified from a named source" (say what was simplified), "our own choice, no source" (thresholds, the role vocabulary), or "measured here".

rulings.title: Cut
rulings.text: Cut: the connect operation by Steiner tree (no recorded question asks for it); the kind-level relevance filter; the redundancy term as a component; the third tier of field contracts (a pass over untyped web JavaScript); the many-feature learned ranker and the calibration step unless the stop rule first survives a simpler test.

rulings.title: Deferred, not built now
rulings.text: Deferred, not built now: the what-breaks ranker (needs test-failure ground truth), the depth-3 tier, the extraction audit with its indexer installs. Per-method confidence is folded into the quality card. Validity sets over the commit graph are infrastructure for stored conclusions and citations, not an agent feature by themselves.

rulings.title: Added because the refuter showed they were missing
rulings.text: Added because the refuter showed they were missing: (a) the primary test set is real lookups taken from recorded sessions, weighted by the tokens they cost, not co-change; (b) an index-only arm (document outline, item-ID lookup, symbol and file index, keyword search, no relation edges) in every test, to isolate what the relations add; (c) a scripted-search arm; (d) a brief written by the orchestrator, and plain heading-and-ID extraction, as the strongest simple competitors for the session-start brief; (e) a task-context store built from what earlier sessions on the same phase read and then edited (the degree-of-interest model of Kersten and Murphy) as the documented competitor to a graph-derived brief; (f) an edit-time warning hook as its own component with a trigger, a cost and a false-alarm rate; (g) two histories: code by commit, documents by content hash, because most program documents are not in version control; (h) a leak rule: every document fact used at a commit is extracted as of that commit; (i) cut rules wherever a test had none.

rulings.title: Build order changes
rulings.text: Build order changes: first the test set of real lookups and the index-only arm; then the document, item, rule and decision layer with the session-start brief (the largest measured cost); then the conclusion ledger, but only after measuring what share of earlier conclusions rest on things inside the repository; the ranking work comes after these because the question it serves (what changes together) is 1.8 % of product lookup cost.

rulings.title: Embeddings and graph neural models
rulings.text: Embeddings and graph neural models: the design says "not at this size" from published evidence and a density argument (about 7 facts per entity here against about 37 in a standard benchmark), not from a measurement on this graph. The owner has trained such models himself. State it as an argued position that can be settled by a small measured trial if he approves the install (a knowledge-graph embedding library and a tensor library, CPU only), and say that the question it would improve is a small part of the token cost.

rulings.title: The decisive test changes
rulings.text: The decisive test changes. An agent pilot of about 40 tasks can only see a saving of about 20 to 25 %, and the plausible effect is single-digit percent of context. So the evidence is built in two steps: a lookup-level replay (recorded lookups answered by each arm, scored on whether the needed span is in the answer and on tokens, which can see small effects), then a focused agent test on the session start, where the measured cost is largest (55 % of carried product lookup tokens are spent before the first edit) and an effect could be large enough to see.

rulings.title: Corrections to what the owner was told earlier
rulings.text: Corrections to what the owner was told earlier, to be shown plainly: (a) the current graph does NOT link calls by name alone (0 of 4,886 call edges; they are resolved by scope, imports and the type checker), so "replace name matching" was wrong; what is true is that 11.2 % of changed definitions had no node (mostly variables and object members); (b) the first test scored "what changes together", which is 1.8 % of product lookup cost; (c) the 60 configurations were compared at a depth where every candidate fitted in the answer, so the ranking could not matter, and at the depth finally chosen the walk reached two thirds of the graph and selected nothing.

design_summary:
DESIGN.md (283 lines) derives graph v2 from the measured competency questions and the documented theory. v2 is a typed property graph used as a knowledge graph in Hogan's sense: a schema derived from competency questions (CQs), stable identity, provenance and a per-build quality card. It adds a temporal layer (validity sets over the commit graph, with premises re-checked on change) and n-ary nodes for change sets, rules with roles, and claims with premise sets. It is not a forecasting TKG, not an embedding model and not a GNN, and the reasons are given with numbers. Model-written content enters only as ledger claims with recorded premises, never as code edges.

Each component states: the theory and its sources, what it replaces in v1, the alternatives rejected, the expected effect, a tuning-data ablation with a stated cut rule, its build cost, its installs and its tier.

The ceiling is stated from the owner's own records. The CQs a graph can serve carry 38 % of product carried tokens (about 8.8 % of product context) and about 21 % of program context. My illustration, not a forecast: with answers one fifth the size of the reads they replace, and half adoption, v2 could move about 3-5 % of product context and about 8 % of program context. It could also cost tokens: CodexGraph used 7-15x the tokens of BM25. Only an agent pilot can show the real share.

Corrections applied from the verifiers:
- 36 edge kinds, 18,875 edge records and 17,410 distinct edges.
- 441 test-to-route records, not 39.
- The ROSE 30-entity cap was a CVS branch-merge filter, not a noise rule.
- The stop rule is demoted to a trial (Adaptive-k scored 73.33 against 76.33-78.00 for fixed budgets).
- Dynamic test edges are demoted to a trial.
- The Moonen et al. figures (8-file cap, 25,000 commits) are unverified and not used.

I built and ran nothing in this lane; the numbers come from the lane notes and verifier notes.
refute_verdict:
The design is a real improvement on v1, but its claim that every choice comes from documented theory does not hold yet. It starts from the measured questions, names its sources, carries the verifiers' corrections and keeps the agent pilot as the only test of tokens. Four problems remain.

1. Improvised choices and miscited sources remain:
   - About a dozen thresholds have no source.
   - The M3 role vocabulary is hand-made.
   - S2's stop rule uses the wrong value for F: 695 tokens is what a scripted search read per typed question. Counting the carry over the remaining calls, an avoided search is worth about 13,000 tokens.
   - Three sources are cited for things they do not say:
     - Hogan's knowledge-graph definition is inclusive, so v1 was already a knowledge graph.
     - The in-lists and out-lists cited to de Kleer belong to Doyle's JTMS.
     - S2's "own derivation" is in fact the marginal value theorem and the information patch model.
2. The validation plan drops the use-case lane's own test set: CQ instances taken from transcripts and weighted by carried tokens. So the zero-model evidence again scores co-change truth and hand-written typed questions, not the measured use. The whole ranking stack serves a question that is not among the 16 recorded CQs.
3. Several tuning tests cannot fail, or are biased:
   - The M1 coverage check and the M6 "cut by about a third" rule pass by construction.
   - The Q1 prune test leans toward cutting kinds.
   - The M3 replay leans toward passing.
   - The A1 brief test passes on file names alone.
   - T4 has no threshold.
   - K1, S1, R4 and R5 have no cut rule.
   - R1 re-runs the pilot on the same 65 commits, without the scripted-search arm an agent actually uses.
   - No clean confirmation set remains: the 75 held-out commits are spent, and only 16 commits (10 touching product code) exist after the frozen commit.
4. The decisive agent pilot, as round 2 sized it (about 40 tasks), detects only savings of about 20 to 25 %. The design's own illustration is 3 to 5 % of product context.

Leak paths the design does not close:
- Hand-assigned invariant roles taken from today's CLAUDE.md text, which names later migrations and PRs.
- Held-out-period snapshots inside the "tuning data".
- In-sample transcript replays: the same 13 sessions produced the question list and would score the brief.

Most program documents are off the commit history: 1,780 untracked files against 124 tracked. So T1/T4 cannot cover most of the 1,147M program carried tokens, and CQ1 conclusions mostly rest on unverifiable premises such as papers, web pages and scratch measurements.

Components that hold up: the storage choice, the not-worth-it list, A1's no-query-language/no-paging stance, K1/K2/K5/K6, T2/T5 and the R1 measurement itself.
